A September 1956 CIA report describes Hungarian public demonstrations growing into a political crisis. Street protests that autumn were swelling beyond anything the regime had faced. Within weeks they would grow into the full revolution of October.

The report tracks the crisis from its first public signs: crowds, demands, and a government losing control of the streets. Demonstration reports mattered because they measured pressure that official statements hid. For readers, this paper stands near the head of the Hungary file of 1956. It marks the point where private discontent became public action. The agency began reporting a revolution in the making rather than mere unrest.

cia-0000132431:
Cuban-Soviet relations are examined in a CIA document dated January 3, 1960. Havana and Moscow were still feeling each other out at that point. Analysts watched every meeting and public statement for signs of a firmer commitment between the two governments.

Within months the careful courtship turned into a working alliance of trade, arms, and advisers. The document tracks its early steps, before either side had promised much in public. For readers, it captures the opening of a partnership that would shape the Cold War in the Americas. Few relationships of the era carried heavier consequences for Washington or lasted so long.

Gibraltar came back before the UN General Assembly in Resolution 2231, passed in December 1966. Spain and Britain, the administering power, had each stated their case, and people from the territory had been heard. The text recalls the 1964 push for talks and the Assembly's own call of the year before.

The Assembly regrets the slow pace of decolonization for the port colony. It calls on both sides to keep talking, with the good of the people of Gibraltar in mind, and asks Britain to speed the process. The sovereignty fight behind the talks, Spain against Britain, runs on to this day.
un-ga-res-a-69-31:
Space belongs to peaceful work, states Resolution A/69/31, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. All states share a stake in the study and use of space, the Moon, and other far bodies, for peaceful ends alone. Such work must serve the good of all lands, rich or poor in wealth and science. The text recalls the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, which bars mass-kill arms from orbit and from the Moon.

No state may use or threaten force in its dealings, in space as on earth, the Charter's rule recalled here. The 1978 disarmament session had held that fresh steps are needed to bar an arms race in space. This yearly vote keeps that guard in place.

plos-pone-0000031:
Ivan Nagaev, Maria Bokarewa, Andrej Tarkowski, and co-authors redefined a hormone-like protein called resistin in work published in 2006. Resistin was first studied in fat tissue and linked to insulin resistance. The human version, this team showed, behaves differently: it is a systemic, immune-derived proinflammatory cytokine, a body-wide alarm signal made by immune cells.

They found resistin targets both leukocytes, the white blood cells, and adipocytes, the fat cells. That makes it a messenger running between the immune system and fat tissue, two systems medicine once treated as separate. Inflammation that involves both helps explain diseases like diabetes and heart disease, and resistin sits at that crossroads in humans.

frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d31: One day after Stalin's reply, Roosevelt wrote to him again, on September 9, 1943. The letter is Document 31 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Back-and-forth at this speed shows the summit planning gathering pace as autumn began. The record gives sender, receiver, and date, and no subject line. Readers will find the message in the Foreign Relations volume, in the sequence that runs from Quebec toward Moscow, Cairo, and Tehran.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d131: Secretary Hull wrote to Minister Kirk in Cairo on November 16, 1943, six days before the Cairo Conference opened in Kirk's city. The letter is Document 131 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Washington-to-host messages in the final week tended to the practical, though this record names no subject. It is printed in the Foreign Relations series, among the papers of the president's voyage and arrival.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d231:
Paper C.C.S. 300/2, issued by the United States Chiefs of Staff aboard the Iowa on 18 November 1943, estimates the enemy situation in the Pacific and Far East for 1944. A long appendix carries the detail, with separate notes on what the Soviets and the Chinese might do.

The estimate expects Japan to stay on the strategic defensive through 1944, striking locally where needed. Tokyo would fight hardest to stop Allied air bases rising in China and to hold Burma, while watching the Soviet border with care. War with the Soviet Union is judged likely only if Japan became convinced that Moscow meant to attack her, or to hand Siberian air bases to the other Allies.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d331:
General Patrick Hurley sent President Roosevelt a second telegram from Tehran on 26 November 1943, following his wire of earlier that day about the Soviet invitation. He had since toured the offered quarters with General Connolly, Secret Service agent Rowley, and Soviet security officers.

The suite sits inside the Russian Embassy compound, in the building Reilly had inspected. It holds six rooms to the left of the entrance, a large reception room, bedrooms, and a dining room. A kitchen below serves the President's staff. It is steam heated, has a private entrance, and stands on the same floor as, and adjoining, the large conference room. Only bathtubs and toilets, removed earlier, need putting back. Hurley judges the quarters far better than the American legation for convenience, communications, and security, while repeating that he told the Russians the legation decision was definite.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d431: President Roosevelt wrote a short letter of welcome to President Ismet Inönü of Turkey from Cairo on 3 December 1943, as Inönü set out for the second Cairo Conference. The letter was carried to Adana by the President's son-in-law, Major John Boettiger. He rode aboard the plane sent to collect the Turkish party. The plane was in the command of Major Otis Bryan. Roosevelt hopes Inönü will have a smooth trip, and says he looks forward with great pleasure to seeing him on Saturday afternoon.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d531:
Lord Halifax, the British ambassador in Washington, wrote to President Roosevelt on December 24, 1943. A Christmas Eve letter from an ambassador to a president was unusual paper, crossing the line between formal business and personal regard. The State Department printed it in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Halifax, a former foreign secretary and viceroy of India, brought great weight to the Washington embassy. His access to Roosevelt was part of the alliance's daily machinery in the capital. For readers, the message shows the British mission working its most important relationship at the highest level, even on a holiday, as the conference season closed.
frus-1944-quebec-d31:
Harry Hopkins wrote to Prime Minister Churchill on August 28, 1944, the first of three messages from him to Churchill bearing that date. The State Department printed them in the Quebec 1944 volume.

Three messages in a day from the President's aide suggest detailed work being finished: the Quebec Conference was a fortnight away, and its arrangements and agenda ran through Hopkins. He wrote as Roosevelt's agent, free to arrange what the President would later approve. For readers, the cluster shows a summit being built piece by piece in late August, in the alliance's most trusted staff channel.
frus-1944-quebec-d131:
London's chiefs of staff cabled General Eisenhower on September 10, 1944, with an urgent request about Warsaw. The British ambassador in Moscow had reported the Soviet position. Moscow was willing to cooperate in supply drops if the aid followed a prearranged plan, and His Majesty's Government wanted no chance of helping the Poles to be missed.

The chiefs asked Eisenhower to consider mounting a supply-drop operation at the earliest possible date. British representatives in Moscow had been told of the Russian decision and asked to make the needed arrangements. Eisenhower was to inform General Deane, the American mission chief in Moscow, of his decision and his requirements from the Russians.
frus-1944-quebec-d231:
The secretaries of the Combined Chiefs drafted the implementing messages on September 12, 1944, as C.C.S. 618/4. Identical letters, adjusted for the recipient, were proposed for Generals Burrows and Deane, the British and American mission chiefs in Moscow. Each man was to propose the tripartite Military Committee to the Soviet General Staff at once.

The message to Deane stresses the limits: the committee would be purely consultative, unable to decide anything without reference home. It must not impinge on the European Advisory Commission's work. A cardinal point was that the Russian member be a senior General Staff officer. With the three armies approaching each other, Deane was told to act immediately so the committee could function soon.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d31: From Moscow on 26 December 1944, Harriman sent Roosevelt a report the day after Christmas. It is document 31 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Malta and Yalta conferences, published by the Department of State. His holiday-week reporting kept Washington current on Soviet attitudes at a moment when the president was weighing what could realistically be achieved at Yalta in February.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d131:
Writing from Warm Springs, Georgia, on 4 December 1944, President Roosevelt gave the State Department three points to keep in the linings of their hats. His short memorandum to Secretary Stettinius is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It answers the summary of British views sent on 29 November.

Germany, he says, should be let back industrially far enough to meet her own needs. But she should do no exporting for some time, until we see how things work out. Second, “we are against reparations.” Third, “we do want restitution of looted property of all kinds.” The one-page note cut across months of staff argument in the President's plainest style.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d231:
Stettinius told Harriman on 30 October 1944 to put the Soviet government straight on Iran. His secret cable, number 2566, is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. Soviet press articles and statements by Mr. Kavtaradze had shown Moscow's annoyance at Iran's freeze on oil talks.

Harriman is to say that Washington noticed the annoyance. He is also to lay out what the American embassy in Tehran was told to convey. The American firms chasing a concession in southern Iran were disappointed, but Washington expressed confidence in Iran's good faith. When talks resume, American firms expect treatment no worse than any other foreigner's. The policy, the cable begins to explain, rests on respect for the sovereign right of an independent nation.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d331:
Dinner talk at Yalta on February 4, 1945, turned serious in its last half hour, and Bohlen's minutes preserve it. Most of the evening was general and personal. Stalin, Roosevelt, and Churchill stayed in very good humor. Then the talk drifted to the rights of small powers in the peace body planned for after the war.

Stalin made his view plain more than once. The three great powers had borne the brunt of the war. They had freed the small states from German rule. So, he argued, they should hold the right to keep the peace. No lesser state, he implied, could have an equal say. The minutes catch a core Yalta dispute surfacing over dinner.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d431:
Article by article, officials took apart the prisoner-of-war draft on February 9, 1945, and this memorandum records the examination. The preamble drew no comment. Neither did Article I. Then the Soviet negotiator, Novikov, began asking for changes in wording.

In Article II, one phrase should be replaced so each side would take the necessary steps to implement the agreement. Elsewhere, transfers should be effected as a rule by agreement, or only after notice to the competent authorities. For Article III, Novikov preferred the Soviet draft's text. The record is dry, clause by clause. It is also where the repatriation bargain took its final legal shape.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d31:
Truman sent a second envoy in this telegram to Churchill of May 22, 1945. He was asking Joseph E. Davies to come to London ahead of the pending three-power conference. A number of matters needed exploring with Churchill, which Truman preferred not to handle by cable. Davies would be in London probably on the twenty-fifth.

He asked Churchill to see Davies at his convenience. The wire, sent by Navy channels, ran in parallel with the Hopkins mission to Moscow. Together the two journeys — Davies west-facing, Hopkins east-facing — prepared the ground for Potsdam by personal talk rather than paper.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d131:
Acting Secretary Grew noted a British hope for early talks in a memorandum dated July 7, 1945. The memo is document 131 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. John Balfour of the British Embassy had called that morning about the coming meeting of heads of government in Berlin.

Balfour said his government very much hoped one or more Americans bound for Berlin might pass through London first. That way, the two sides could talk over matters coming up at the main meeting. He knew Washington would not want the Russians to think the two were ganging up on them, but thought lower-level experts could come quietly. Grew replied that feeling in the American group ran against such early talks, though he would look into it at once. Nothing in the record shows the visit happening.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d231:
Ambassador Winant handed the foreign ministers proposal to Anthony Eden in a letter dated July 8, 1945. The letter is document 231 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It transmits the draft the President planned to present to Churchill and Stalin early in their talks.

Things fall, move, and appear where they should not in Fort's third book, Lo, of 1931. Teleportation is his word and his theme: matter shifted by a force no law yet names. Poltergeists, falls from clear skies, and wild shifts of place fill the file.

Fort piles case on case from the news of the world, each with its date and source. His tone is drier and his aim surer than in the first books. Lo is the damned data at its strangest and most pure. Few books make the world feel so thin at the seams.
frankenstein-1831:
Mary Shelley took her famed novel in hand once more and made this new form in 1831. It is the text most readers have known since that year. She added a long new start, in which she tells how the tale came to her in 1816.

The frame of the tale is reworked, and Victor's fate bears a more dark and fixed cast. The being he made stands in a more grave light, and the blame shifts in tone. This is Frankenstein as Shelley at last chose to leave it to the world.
spee-cautio-criminalis-1631:
Friedrich Spee was a German Jesuit priest who heard the last words of many women judged as witches. In 1631 he put out Cautio Criminalis in Latin, with no name on the title page. The book was the first strong Catholic attack on the witch trials. Spee risked his post and his life to write it.

Spee shows how torture forces false claims from weak and strong alike. He asks judges to test proof with care and to doubt paid witch finders. His calm case helped slow the trials in parts of Germany. Few books of the age speak for the accused with such force.
kingsborough-mexico-vol-1-1831:
Lord Kingsborough gave his wealth and health to one vast work. The Antiquities of Mexico, Book One, came out in 1831. Edward King, Lord Kingsborough, held that the Jews were kin to the folk of old Mexico. The set runs to nine books of plates and text.

Book One gives fine copies of Mexican paintings and glyph texts. Kingsborough paid skilled hands to copy codices from stores all over Europe. Most of the source books have since been lost or harmed. The set is a chief store of the art of old Mexico.

limborch-history-of-the-inquisition-vol-:
Philipp van Limborch, a Dutch Protestant scholar, published his Historia Inquisitionis in 1692, the classic early account of the tribunal. Samuel Chandler translated it into English in 1731, and this is the first volume. Limborch built his history on the archives of the Inquisition of Toulouse, which had come into his hands.

He traces the rise of persecution from the early church through the Albigensian wars to the standing tribunal. His tone is grave and fair for his age, and his documents do the accusing. Protestant Europe read Limborch as the standard proof of Rome's cruelty. The work shaped every history of the Inquisition written for two centuries.

The second volume of Samuel Chandler's 1731 English Limborch is the documentary heart of the work. Philipp van Limborch printed here the Book of Sentences of the Inquisition of Toulouse, the Liber Sententiarum, as his appendix of proof. The first volume told the history; this one shows the papers.

Sentence by sentence, the record names men and women of Languedoc, their alleged errors, and their punishments: penances, crosses worn on the coat, prison, the stake. The years covered run from 1307 to 1323, under the inquisitor Bernard Gui and his fellows. Few books bring the medieval tribunal so close. Limborch let the archive speak, and it still does.
paley-works-complete-1831:
William Paley, an English clergyman and Cambridge teacher, wrote the books that a generation of students learned their morals and their faith from. The complete Works in one volume, Philadelphia, 1831, gather his Life, his Moral and Political Philosophy, and his Evidences of Christianity. His Natural Theology stands with them, along with the Horae Paulinae, his Tracts, Sermons, and the Clergyman's Companion.

Paley writes with a gift for the clear example and the homely comparison that any reader can follow. His watchmaker argument for God's design, from Natural Theology, became the most famous of its kind. His moral philosophy grounds duty in God's will and human happiness. One volume here holds a whole curriculum of Georgian faith.
alkhwarizmi-algebra-rosen-1831:
Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi wrote the founding text of algebra in ninth century Baghdad. Frederic Rosen translated the Arabic work into English in 1831 for the Oriental Translation Fund. The edition prints the English alongside the Arabic. Algebra takes its very name from the book's Arabic title word, al-jabr.

Al-Khwarizmi teaches how to solve equations by restoring and balancing both sides. He sorts problems into types and works each one with clear rules. Trade, inheritance, and land measure supply his practice cases. The book carried Hindu-Arabic methods toward Europe through later copies. Readers meet a science at its birth. The voice is calm and practical.
audubon-ornithological-biography-vol1-18:
John James Audubon painted the birds of America, and his Ornithological Biography supplies their written lives. Volume one appeared in 1831 as the text companion to his great picture work. Audubon writes species accounts from years of field watching. Habits, nests, song, and range fill each account with fresh detail.

Frontier tales run between the science, drawn from his travels in wild America. He shot, drew, and watched birds from Labrador to the Gulf shores. The mix of story and study made the volumes famous on two continents. Volume one opens a five volume companion set. Readers who know the prints meet their author here. His energy fills every page.
plos-pone-0003431:
David A. Shoham and colleagues linked sugary soda to a kidney warning sign in this 2008 study. Kidney failure rates rose after high fructose corn syrup spread through American food. Soda sweetened with sugar is a main source of fructose. The team used a large national health survey from 1999 to 2004.

They looked for albuminuria, protein leaking into urine, an early sign of kidney damage. Soda intake and that warning sign moved together in the data. The link was statistical, from survey records, not a trial. Still, it adds weight to concerns about fructose and kidney health.
plos-pone-0003531:
Gabriela Durcova-Hills and co-authors turned germ cells back into stem cells in this 2008 paper. Primordial germ cells are the early source of eggs and sperm. They begin as flexible epiblast cells, then lock into the germ line. A complex with Blimp1 helps set and keep that locked state.

Yet germ cells can be induced to reopen their options. The team reprogrammed them into pluripotent stem cells. Such cells can form many body tissues, not just gametes. The conversion offers a new route to versatile lab stem cells. Stem cells from germ lines may dodge some of the moral debates over embryos.
plos-pone-0003631:
René C. W. Mandl, Hugo G. Schnack, Marcel P. Zwiers, and colleagues published this brain imaging study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Standard scans show which gray matter areas switch on during a task. They say little about activity along the white matter tracts that link those areas.

The team measured changes in fractional anisotropy, a sign of how water moves along nerve fibers, while people did tasks. Those changes tracked activity along the tracts themselves. The method, called functional diffusion tensor imaging, opens a way to watch the brain's wiring at work, not just its hubs.
plos-pone-0003731:
John P. Norman, Seth W. Perry, Holly M. Reynolds, and colleagues published this brain study in PLOS ONE in 2008. HIV-1 causes neurologic disease that modern drug therapy cannot fully cure. The virus is never fully cleared from the central nervous system, and normal neural signaling gets disrupted there.

The team studied Tat, a protein the virus makes, in neurons. Tat switched on ryanodine receptors, releasing calcium inside the cells. That set off the unfolded protein response and pushed mitochondria into an abnormal state, a chain that helps explain lasting brain injury in HIV.
plos-pone-0003831:
Susanne Hartmann, John H. Missimer, Cornelia Stoeckel, and colleagues published this brain imaging study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Telling objects apart by touch is an essential human skill. It relies on communication between motor, touch, and higher-order brain areas. Such spread-out networks are hard to study with simple subtraction methods.

The team used principal component analysis on fMRI data from a tactile discrimination task. That approach extracts the connected patterns behind performance. Their analysis shows tactile knowing as a conversation across the brain, not the job of a single touch area.
plos-pone-0003931:
Elise Drouyer, Ouria Dkhissi-Benyahya, Christophe Chiquet, and co-authors studied glaucoma and the body clock in 2008. Glaucoma is a common eye disease and a major cause of blindness. It slowly destroys the optic nerve and the retinal cells that feed it. Most study had focused on vision loss itself.

Their PLOS ONE article asks what the disease does to daily timing. Retinal cells also send light signals that set the circadian clock. Damage to them could disturb sleep and daily rhythms in patients. The work widens glaucoma care beyond eyesight alone. The full report sits in PLOS ONE, free to read with all its data shown.
plos-pone-0004031:
Caterina I. Fanello, Corine Karema, Pamela Avellino, and co-authors flagged a malaria drug risk in 2008. G6PD deficiency is the most common inherited enzyme defect in humans. It gives some protection against malaria itself. It also makes red cells break down under oxidant drugs.

Their PLOS ONE article reports high risk of severe anemia after one drug mix. The mix was chlorproguanil-dapsone plus artesunate. Patients carrying the G6PD A- variant faced the danger. The warning argues for screening or drug choice changes in such patients. The article came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for science and health research.
plos-pone-0004131:
Jung Joo Hong and colleagues published this immunology study in PLOS ONE in 2009. CD8 T cells are white blood cells that help control viral infections. The team wanted to know exactly where virus-specific T cells sit inside the tissues of monkeys infected with SIV, the monkey form of HIV.

Using MHC class I tetramers, lab tools that tag T cells matching a chosen virus piece, they mapped the cells in lymph and genital tissues. They found distinct local groups of these T cells, including some with low CD8 levels, inside lymphoid follicles and the genital lining. Knowing where the cells gather helps explain how the body fights the virus at its entry points.
plos-pone-0004231:
Roxane Chiori and colleagues published this evolution study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Hox genes pattern the body along its head-to-tail axis in most animals. How early they took on that role, and whether the Hox and ParaHox clusters began before two-sided animals existed, has been hotly debated.

The team studied the hydrozoan jellyfish Clytia hemisphaerica, a cnidarian from a lineage that split off early. They present evidence on whether its Hox genes are involved in axial patterning. A patterning role in such an animal would push the job's origin deep into animal history.
plos-pone-0004331:
Alessandro Bartolomucci and colleagues published this obesity study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Social and psychological factors interact with genes and diet in determining obesity, yet few pre-clinical studies address psychosocial factors in metabolic disorders. The team's own earlier work in male mice had shown chronic social stress changing body weight.

Here they examined the metabolic consequences of that stress and the mice's vulnerability to diet-induced obesity. Stressed males facing rich food model a very human situation. The study asks whether social defeat makes the body store fat differently, before any new drug is considered.

cia-0000011831:

Portugal still held Angola and Mozambique, Rhodesia's white government had defied Britain, and South Africa ruled itself and Namibia. Guerrilla groups in each territory were taking up arms with outside backing.

The survey weighs each movement's strength, its leaders, and its ties to communist states. It also judges their chances of winning power in the near term. The paper captures the start of bush wars that would reshape the whole region over the next two decades.

Dinner tables were working ground in Cold War diplomacy. Guest lists, seating, and table talk all carried intelligence value, and officers filed them as carefully as any cipher traffic.

The note preserves the social texture of that world in one line. Even suppers were intelligence, and the files treated them accordingly. For readers, the fragment shows how completely the watchers watched: down to who ate with whom.
cia-0000012831:

The paper totals the bloc's generosity and maps its reach. It weighs credits, weapons, and technicians as moves in one game. For readers, it shows the Cold War fought with rubles as well as rockets, counted by the other side.

plos-pone-0006431: Baby warmth tells a health story. Stern and team found long-range patterns in infant warmth swings. The rhythms flag risky wobbles — tiny bodies, telling signals, tracked, with the first six months key. Breathing linked too, apnea risk flagged: heat control still learning.
plos-pone-0006531: Germs untangle their doubled DNA. Carnoy and Roten mapped dif/Xer systems that resolve DNA bundle twins in Proteobacteria. The cut-and-paste fix, charted — germs' untangling trick, mapped, in the Escherichia coli model. Ten to fifteen percent double up, via XerC and XerD: protein scissors.
plos-pone-0006631: A gene suspect cleared in Silver-Russell. Bernier-Latmani and team found no CTCFL/BORIS mutations in Silver-Russell patients. The imprint region's other story — a negative gene hunt, published, amid IGF2/H19 low tagging. Tag errors, varied disease: no coding defects, ICR1 probed, 50 percent, suspect ruled out.
plos-pone-0009431: Neuroscientists can now switch brain cells on with light, but aiming the beam at many cells at once has been clumsy. This paper demonstrates holographic photolysis: shaping light into patterns that trigger multiple chosen neurons simultaneously in slices of mouse hippocampus. The technique gives researchers a conductor's baton for brain circuits, letting them play chords of cells instead of single notes.
plos-pone-0009531: Cells run tiny proton pumps called V-ATPases to control acidity, built from many interchangeable parts. With subunits and splice variants multiplying in the literature, this paper proposes a unified naming system. The nomenclature clears up a confusing corner of cell biology, giving every pump part one clear name.
plos-pone-0009631: The enzyme NADPH oxidase helps immune cells make germ-killing oxidants — but too much inflammation can harm the lungs. This mouse study finds the enzyme also puts limits on innate immune responses in the lungs. The paper reveals a built-in throttle on lung inflammation, with lessons for a rare inherited immune disorder.
plos-pone-0010431: Flat dishes poorly mimic prostate tumors. This study builds a comprehensive panel of 3D prostate cell models for studying growth, invasion, and drug response. The paper offers more lifelike tools for a common cancer. Better models mean better drugs, tested in more realistic tumors.
plos-pone-0010531: Stem cells keep their DNA loosely packed — until they commit to a fate. This study maps chromatin architecture in the early mouse embryo. The paper reveals how genome packaging reflects a cell's remaining potential. The maps show potential written directly into DNA packaging.
plos-pone-0010631: HIV and hepatitis C travel together. This Chinese study measures HCV prevalence and genetic diversity among HIV-positive people in high-risk groups. The paper maps a dual epidemic that complicates treatment. The survey guides treatment where the two viruses overlap.
plos-pone-0010731: Melanoma's toughest cells resist drugs — but which marker flags them? This study tests whether ALDH enzyme activity marks the most aggressive melanoma cells. It doesn't. The paper rules out a popular candidate. The negative finding redirects the hunt for true markers.
plos-pone-0010831: Ground beetles eat weed seeds — with microbial help. This study shows bacterial gut symbionts help an omnivorous beetle digest seeds. The paper reveals a digestive partnership. The finding could improve biological weed control. The partnership turns beetles into weed fighters.
plos-pone-0010931: Misaligned eyes don't just blur vision — they rewire the brain. This study uses brain imaging to find dorsal visual pathway changes in comitant exotropia patients. The paper reveals strabismus's neural footprint. The finding informs treatment timing. The footprint shows the brain adapting to crossed eyes.
plos-pone-0011031: Popping Tylenol during MS therapy might mute the drug. This study shows acetaminophen alters the gene-expression response to recombinant interferon-beta. The paper flags a common drug interaction. The finding advises caution with over-the-counter painkillers. The caution matters for millions of patients.
plos-pone-0011131: Chronic jaw pain may begin in the muscle's stretch sensors. This rat study assesses whether muscle spindle mechanoreceptor afferents drive chronic masseter muscle pain. The paper probes a pain pathway. The finding could guide new pain therapies. The therapies could ease temporomandibular disorders.
plos-pone-0011231: Brain tumors may betray themselves through sticky proteins. This study looks at cell-stickiness molecules in meningioma samples. The paper reveals a telling pattern. The finding could sharpen brain-tumor diagnosis. The sharper diagnosis guides surgery and care. The care saves lives and brain function.
plos-pone-0011331: Tree-dwelling ants lasso giant prey with Velcro-like grips. This study shows arboreal ants use the Velcro principle — tiny hooks — to capture very large prey. The paper reveals a hunting adaptation. The finding aids entomology. The aided entomology marvels at nature's engineering.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1231:
Sato answered Tokyo on 21 July 1945, the same day as the minister's twin cables. The Moscow envoy's reports formed a steady answer to Togo's hopes: polite Soviet phrases, no firm word, no date for an envoy's hearing. Time favored Moscow, not Tokyo.

Sato read the delay rightly as a kind of answer. His cables grew blunter as the week wore on, urging Tokyo to face facts. This dispatch sits in that sequence. It is part of the hidden record at Potsdam. The Allied leaders read this enemy traffic each morning, while they set the terms Japan would soon receive.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1331:
Assistant Secretary Dunn wrote to the Secretary of State on 23 July 1945. Dunn was among the most seasoned career envoys on the American team. His notes carried staff judgment to the chief in the middle of the talks.

A message from Dunn at Potsdam joined two layers: the working staff and the man who bargained for the United States. It could fix a stand, report a talk, or ready the chief's next move. This one dates from the second week's start. It shows the professional core of the team at work, in the plain channel of a note to the secretary.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1431:
The Soviet delegation submitted another text on 29 July 1945, the third of that date in the volume's closing pages. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

Three texts in a day from one delegation is a drafting offensive. As Potsdam wound down, the Soviet side worked to lock its gains into the conference's papers before the leaders left Germany. Readers can follow the effort across this cluster and into the protocol. The texts also show the limits of paper power. Some Soviet wording was taken, some was fought to a draw. The difference between the two is the summit's true result.
frus-1945-50-intel-d31:
Donald Russell, assistant secretary of state for administration, wrote to McCormack, the special assistant for research and intelligence, on 22 October 1945. Both men served in the State Department. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

Russell ran the department's housekeeping: people, money, and space. McCormack's new intelligence office needed all three at once, having just absorbed the OSS analysts. An inside paper from the administration chief to the intelligence chief shows the unglamorous work of housing a new function. Readers often skip such papers, yet they decide whether bright plans live or die. This one shows the State Department's intelligence office being built from the inside.
frus-1945-50-intel-d131:
Russell, assistant secretary of state for administration, sent an instruction to Alling, the American minister in Tangier, on 3 January 1947. Instructions from the department direct a post's conduct. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

Tangier appears in both volumes of this slice of history: a Potsdam question in 1945, and a post receiving department instructions in 1947. The paper belongs to the volume's State thread, where intelligence business touched ordinary diplomacy in small ports. Readers can take it as a sign of the system's settling. The secret work of the postwar world now ran through channels as plain as an administration chief's instruction to a minister in North Africa.
frus-1945-50-intel-d231:
The General Counsel of the Central Intelligence Agency (Houston) addressed a memorandum to Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter on 7 April 1948. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 231 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. The young CIA was still defining its job, while the Council weighed how far secret action abroad should go.

A short memo could set a meeting, kill a plan, or start one. This one played its part in that daily traffic. Whole policies can be traced through chains of such notes, each one moving the matter a step. Alone it is a page; in sequence it is evidence of how a state taught itself a new trade.
frus-1945-50-intel-d331:
A memorandum dated 20 November 1947 links two senior offices. The sender was the Secretary of State’s Special Assistant for Research and Intelligence (Armstrong). The reader was Acting Secretary of State Lovett. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 331 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. The old board and its group were gone, replaced that fall by the CIA under the new National Security Council.

The value of the form is its speed: a page or two, a clear ask, and a name at the top to answer for it. Kept in sequence, such memos form the true diary of the office that sent them. Read next to the papers around it in the volume, it helps show how the postwar intelligence system took shape step by step.
frus-1945-50-intel-d431:
On 6 January 1950 the National Security Council issued Intelligence Directive No. 12. The text is document 431 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Two directives on one day point to a full agenda at the start of 1950. The Council used the numbered series to keep every agency inside one frame. Read beside Directive No. 11, this order shows the steady, formal way the early Cold War state managed its secret work. Issued as a pair, the two January orders divided fresh duties between the same set of agencies. The pair shows the Council at its most brisk, settling two points in a single day.
frus-1861-d31:
On 30 July 1861, William H. Seward wrote to Henry Sanford, his envoy in Belgium. The letter is document 31 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

The Union defeat at Bull Run on 21 July shook faith at home and abroad. Seward now had to hold foreign courts steady while the army rebuilt. A letter to Brussels nine days after the battle belongs to that work of repair and resolve. After Bull Run, Seward's aim was to show a Union shaken but far from beaten. Resolve, repeated in plain words, was the coin Seward paid out all that autumn.
frus-1861-d131:
On 17 June 1861, William H. Seward wrote to William Dayton in a settled, watchful tone. The letter is document 131 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Mid June letters from Seward have a settled feel: the lines are set, the work is watch and ward. His note to Dayton keeps Paris inside the same firm frame as London. The two posts, read together, formed the Union's wall in Europe. London and Paris, held in one frame, left the South no great door into Europe. No great door left open meant no great hope left alive for the South in Europe.
frus-1861-d231:
Orders from Washington reached James Shepherd Pike in a State Department letter dated 16 May 1861. It stands as Document 231 in the volume of foreign papers laid before Congress with the President's message. By then, in the opening months of the Civil War, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d31:
Orders from Washington reached Charles Francis Adams in a State Department letter dated 11 March 1862. It stands as Document 31 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. It was written in the winter of the war's second year, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d131:
The home office spoke to Charles Francis Adams on 18 August 1862, through a letter from Seward. It stands as Document 131 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. It was written in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d231:
The second Stuart letter of 2 September 1862 stands as Document 231 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. William Stuart, acting head of the British legation, sent both letters to Secretary of State William H. Seward.

Two letters in a day from the legation suggest several live matters at once, each kept on its own sheet by custom. Early September 1862 gave the legation plenty to handle: invasion news, shaken markets, and fresh instructions to seek from London. Paired letters like these show formal business keeping its order in a disordered week. Cases under such notes were often small: one ship, one prisoner, one point of form.
frus-1862-d331:
William L. Dayton reported from Paris on 6 October 1862 in a letter printed as Document 331 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It went to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington.

By the time Dayton wrote, the Emancipation Proclamation's text was known in Paris and French opinion was stirring. Working-class sympathy for the Union grew harder for the emperor to ignore. Dayton's report that week fed Washington's sense that the proclamation was doing diplomatic work no envoy could have done alone. Paris and London consulted each other often before either acted on the American war. Dayton's French was limited, and he leaned on his staff and on careful written notes.
frus-1862-d431:
On 16 July 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this reply to Gabriel García Tassara, the Spanish minister in Washington. It stands as Document 431 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Mid-July 1862 was a low point for Union arms, with McClellan driven back from Richmond. Foreign ministers in Washington watched for signs that the government might bend, and Seward's notes had to show no bend at all. His exchange with Tassara kept Spain at formal arm's length on the war while handling the standing business between the two countries. The letter is a sample of Seward's desk diplomacy in the war's hardest summer.
frus-1862-d531:
On 7 June 1862, the same day the Dutch minister's two notes were dated, Secretary of State William H. Seward answered Roest van Limburg. The reply is Document 531 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Same-day answers were Seward's specialty when a matter was warm, and the Dutch file in June 1862 was warm indeed. His reply kept the exchange moving without conceding the Union's reading of its belligerent rights at sea. The Netherlands, whose trade the blockade touched daily, pressed its points through Van Limburg with equal energy. Read in sequence from Document 527, the June letters form a compact case study in how wartime questions between friendly governments were actually worked through.
frus-1862-d631:
On 6 May 1862 Edward Joy Morris sent this report from Constantinople to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It is Document 631 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, accompanying the President's annual message.

Morris's May report came from the far end of the Department's world in a season of Union advance. At the Ottoman court the American war was by then a settled topic: a great republic was fighting its rebels, and the powers watched. His dispatch kept the record of American business at the Porte complete for the spring. Read with the instructions Seward sent him, it shows a mature posting running itself, with Washington informed at intervals and local judgment trusted in between.
frus-1863p1-d31:
On 16 January 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams in London. The letter is document 31 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. Seward's January mail to the legation runs thick in this part of the volume.

The secretary wrote to keep Adams's hand strong in talks with Lord Russell. Each letter restated the Union's claims and fed the envoy the facts he needed from home. This one falls between Adams's reports of mid-January, a sign of how tight the loop had grown. It is a plain working sheet, and its worth is in the chain it holds together.
frus-1863p1-d131:
On 26 March 1863, Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward for the second time that day. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 131 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The mate to a dispatch often held what the first had no room for. Adams's pair of 26 March closed the legation's mail for a crowded week. This letter is its second half. With the Seward sheet of the same date set just before the pair in the volume, the cluster shows the sea mail at its busiest. Two pens worked one war, an ocean apart.
frus-1863p1-d231:
Writing from London on 10 July 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, reported to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. The dispatch is document 231 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

Public meetings across Britain, many of them backing the Union and emancipation, formed part of the picture Adams reported. He tracked opinion as carefully as he tracked ministers. Read alongside its neighbors in the volume, it shows the daily grind behind the war's big diplomatic crises.
frus-1863p1-d331:
The American answer to London on 3 December 1862 took the form of this note from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. It is document 331 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

Lyons was the man Seward had to persuade, warn, or answer in person in Washington. Notes to him carried the American side of each dispute between the two governments. The letter's value lies partly in its place in the sequence: it shows the conversation between the two capitals continuing without a break.
frus-1863p1-d431:
The letter printed as document 431 was written on 28 March 1863 by William H. Seward to Lord Lyons. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. The letter is one piece of the steady stream of notes that passed between the two governments in the spring of 1863. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily.

Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page.
frus-1863p1-d531:
William H. Seward, the Secretary of State wrote this official letter to Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington on 23 May 1862. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863.

Confederate warships built in British yards were a sore point all year. Washington pressed London to stop them, and letters like this carried that pressure. Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d631:
Dated 16 October 1863, document 631 is a letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war? Such notes moved by hand between the State Department and the British legation, a few streets apart in wartime Washington.

The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. The stakes behind this routine mail were high. If Britain had backed the Confederacy, the war could have changed course, so each note helped hold the line of British neutrality. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
plos-pbio-0020031:
Yi Tang, Taek Soon Lee, and Chaitan Khosla reported a bioengineering feat in PLOS Biology in 2004. Certain soil microbes build useful drugs, like the antibiotic tetracycline, with huge enzymes called polyketide synthases. These enzymes link small building blocks into ring-shaped products, step by step.

The team rebuilt the system with two-part enzymes so they could steer where changes land on the final product. Controlled changes are the hard part of making new versions of old drugs. Their success shows that these assembly lines can be reprogrammed with care. That opens a path to custom compounds that nature never made, some of which might beat drug-resistant germs.
plos-pbio-0020131:
Michael S. Kobor, Shivkumar Venkatasubramanyan, and their team studied a histone-swapping machine in yeast for PLOS Biology in 2004. DNA wraps around proteins called histones. A variant spool, H2A.Z, takes the place of the standard one at certain genes and changes how they behave.

The study names the protein complex that loads H2A.Z into place. Its core is an enzyme called Swr1p, kin to a family of DNA-moving motors. Knowing the machine explains how cells place the variant with care rather than at random. H2A.Z placement affects gene activity across many species, including humans. The yeast work gives a parts list that other fields can build on.
plos-pbio-0020231:
James M. Holaska, Amy K. Kowalski, Katherine L. Wilson, and their team studied a nucleus protein in PLOS Biology in 2004. Emerin sits in the inner membrane of the cell nucleus. Mutations in emerin cause a form of muscular dystrophy that also harms the heart.

The team found that emerin caps the pointed end of actin filaments, the thin rods that give cells shape. That job hints at a network of actin right against the nucleus. Such a network could help the nucleus hold its form and place. The finding gives a fresh angle on how emerin faults weaken muscle cells. It also adds the nucleus to the map of the cell's inner scaffolding.
plos-pone-0000131:
Sara O. Dean and James A. Spudich published this cell division study in PLOS ONE in 2006. Using Drosophila S2 cells, a fruit fly cell line, they examine how the motor protein myosin is recruited to the cell's equator during division. The focus is on an enzyme called Rho kinase and the chemical tag it places on myosin's light chain.

As the title states, Rho kinase's job in this recruitment is to phosphorylate that light chain, switching myosin on at the right place. Getting this step right is what lets a dividing cell pinch in two. The paper clarifies one link in the machinery of mitosis, the process behind growth and tissue repair.
plos-pone-0000231:
Tianshou Zhou, Jiajun Zhang, Zhanjiang Yuan, and colleagues published this theory paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Many natural systems tick in rhythm, from firing neurons to flashing fireflies, and outside stimuli can push groups into shared rhythm. The authors study how external stimuli mediate such collective rhythms and propose artificial control strategies for them.

Controlling group rhythm matters in fields from power grids to brain stimulation. The authors model when an outside signal can steer a population of oscillators. Their strategies offer a handle on synchronization, the same phenomenon that can help a system work or, in a brain, produce a seizure.
plos-pone-0000331:
Jeffrey Shaman and Jonathan F. Day published this mosquito ecology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Mosquito populations breed in phases tied to reproduction. The authors show that these populations lock their reproductive phase to the frequency of rainfall, syncing breeding pulses with how often rain falls.

Rain creates the standing water mosquitoes need, so syncing to its rhythm is adaptive. The authors model and document that phase locking. Predicting mosquito pulses matters for controlling diseases they carry, from dengue to West Nile, because control works best timed to breeding. That rhythm gives control programs a clock to work against.
plos-pone-0000431:
Ulrike Böer and colleagues watched stress rewrite gene activity in mouse brains, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The mice were engineered so that genes driven by the CRE/CREB system light up, making their activity visible. Under chronic social stress, that system drove gene expression up, and the team tested whether antidepressant treatment could reverse the change.

The authors report that antidepressant treatment did reverse the stress-driven rise. A visible readout of a stress-sensitive gene system lets researchers screen how stress and drugs interact in the living brain. The findings support the idea that long-term stress reshapes brain chemistry in ways that treatment can push back.
plos-pone-0000531:
Qi Wang and Yuan-Ping Pang tested a docking program's accuracy on a large set of known structures, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Computer docking predicts how a small molecule fits into a protein, a key step in drug design. The EUDOC program reproduced 161 small-molecule complex crystal structures accurately, and the authors proposed expanding its use to supramolecular chemistry.

Reproducing known answers is how a prediction tool earns trust; 161 successes is a serious benchmark. Supramolecular chemistry, the chemistry of molecules binding each other, uses the same fitting logic beyond drugs. A validated program serves both fields, and papers like this are the receipts.
plos-pone-0000631:
Elías Barquero-Calvo, Esteban Chaves-Olarte, David S. Weiss and co-authors explored how Brucella abortus slips past first-line defenses, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Brucella causes brucellosis and can set up chronic, long-lasting infections. The question was how it manages that at the very start of infection.

The team found the bacterium did not trigger proinflammatory responses early on. White blood cells were not recruited, and blood showed no humoral or cellular changes. In short, the innate immune system barely noticed its arrival. That stealth at the onset helps explain how Brucella gains the foothold it needs to persist.
plos-pone-0000731:
Ana Hrus, Gordon Lau, Harald Hutter and colleagues characterized the worm version of a junction protein, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Agrin is a basement membrane protein crucial for building and maintaining the neuromuscular junction in vertebrates, where nerves meet muscle. The C. elegans genome harbors a candidate agrin gene, agr-1. The team cloned its cDNA to determine the protein's structure and where it is expressed.

Their title reports expression in the pharynx, in IL1 neurons, and in distal tip cells. It also reports a negative: worm agrin does not genetically interact with genes for synaptogenesis or muscle function. A clear negative result steers the field away from assuming the worm protein does the vertebrate job.
plos-pone-0000831:
Bruce E. Deagle, Nick J. Gales, Karen Evans and co-authors read penguin menus from droppings instead of stomachs. The usual way to study seabird diet is to flush the stomach and sort what comes up. That is hard on the birds, and hard to arrange on remote islands. The team tested DNA-based analysis of faeces as a kinder route, in a study in PLOS ONE in 2007.

Their test case was macaroni penguins raising chicks. DNA in droppings can name prey that digestion would else hide. If the method works, scientists can sample often, across whole colonies, without handling a single bird. Diet data of that depth feed straight into fishery and wildlife choices in the far south seas.
plos-pone-0000931:
Daniel Kelley, Richard Davidson, Jamie Elliott and colleagues found a key signaling chain altered in fragile X syndrome, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Fragile X is the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability and autism. It comes from a repeat expansion in the fmr1 gene, which lowers a protein the brain needs.

The team focused on the cyclic AMP cascade, a relay that helps nerve cells respond and adapt. Their report says the relay runs differently in the fragile X nervous system. A defined chemical fault gives drug research something concrete to aim at. It also helps explain how one gene change can ripple across learning and behavior.
plos-pone-0001031:
Maja Adamska, Sandie Degnan, Kathryn Green and colleagues found embryo patterning signals at work in a sponge, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Animal development rests on cells sticking together, signaling and cooperating. Sponges sit at the base of the animal tree, so their toolkits hint at what the first animals had.

The team report expression of Wnt and TGF-beta signals in the sponge Amphimedon queenslandica. Both families guide embryonic patterning in later animals. Finding them active in a sponge embryo pushes the origin of patterning to the very start of animal life. The work gives the deep root of development a concrete gene list.
plos-pone-0001131:
A healthy brain notices when a pattern breaks, even when nobody is paying attention. Erich Schröger and colleagues studied that ability in hearing for a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Their brain recordings show that violations of abstract sound rules are processed even when the sounds are ignored.

The team tested rules that go beyond single tones, such as patterns spanning several sounds. Subjects did another task while the sounds played, yet their brains still registered rule-breaking events. Encoding rules and catching violations outside focused attention is vital for adaptive behavior. As the authors note, it lets an organism react to change without watching for it.
plos-pone-0001231:
Biologists increasingly struggle to agree on what a gene is. Evelyn Fox Keller and David Harel take up that disarray in a 2007 PLOS ONE article titled Beyond the Gene. The classical concept, a neat stretch of DNA coding for one product, has been eroded by decades of findings.

After reviewing the problems, the authors propose an alternative to both the concept and the word. Their essay is a piece of conceptual analysis rather than an experiment. It matters because how scientists define the gene shapes how genomes are annotated, taught, and discussed in public.
plos-pone-0001331:
Theiler's virus is a mouse picornavirus that infects neurons and, unusually, passes from their axons into the surrounding myelin sheath. Jean-Pierre Roussarie and colleagues studied that transfer in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Earlier work had shown the virus trafficking from the axon of infected neurons into myelin.

When this traffic is interrupted, as in the shiverer mouse, which carries a mutation in the myelin basic protein gene, the infection's course changes. The authors examine axon-to-myelin transfer of a non-enveloped virus, a route without obvious machinery. Theiler's virus is also a model for multiple sclerosis, which gives the work a second audience.
plos-pone-0001431:
Joan Company and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on climate and life in the deep sea. Life on the deep floor was thought to live on scraps that sink from the sunlit zone. Side flow of scraps from land edges may matter too, but was less known. The team tracked deep sea numbers against climate shifts.

They found that climate swings shape deep populations in a clear way. Shifts in wind and rain change the flow of food to the depths. That link makes deep life less cut off from the world above than once thought. It also means climate change may reach the deep sea faster than expected.
plos-pone-0001531:
Antonio Pacheco and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on causes of death in HIV patients in Brazil. Brazil was the first developing land to give free HIV drugs to all in 1996. Deaths fell, but how the mix of causes shifted was not logged. The team assessed death records in the drug era.

They found a rise in deaths from ills not tied to AIDS itself. As HIV care lets people live longer, heart, liver, and other ills take a larger share. Care plans must thus widen past HIV alone. The study marks a shift in what clinics in Brazil now most need.
plos-pone-0001631:
Jason R. Gerstner, Quentin Z. Bremer, William M. Vander Heyden, and their co-authors tracked a brain protein across the day in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The protein is Fabp7, short for brain fatty acid binding protein. It plays a role in early growth of the nervous system. In adult brain it is found in support cells called astrocytes and in young nerve cell precursors.

The team reports that levels of the Fabp7 gene's message in adult mouse brain rise and fall over a 24-hour cycle. A related protein, Fabp5, does not show the same pattern. The full text gives the time-course data from the hippocampus and other brain areas. Daily rhythms in brain support cells may shape how the brain handles fats, sleep, and the birth of new nerve cells.
plos-pone-0001731:
Ying Yu and co-authors measured DNA methylation in chickens bred to resist or suffer tumors, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Chickens carry inherited endogenous viruses called ALVE, retrovirus-like elements built into their DNA. These elements correlate negatively with disease resistance, and changes in methylation, chemical tags that silence DNA, may affect susceptibility to neoplastic disease.
